concepts.decision: Start with asset criticality, safety, site threats, utilities, occupancy, and continuity needs.
concepts.definition: Coordinated physical protection of people, sites, assets, operations, and recovery.
concepts.failureExample: A facility plan focuses on locks but ignores flood exposure and emergency egress.
concepts.label: Facility Security

concepts.decision: Layer controls from public space to critical assets based on consequence.
concepts.definition: Controls that deter, delay, detect, assess, respond to, and recover from physical threats.
concepts.failureExample: A locked room has unmanaged visitor access and no alarm response.
concepts.label: Physical Security

concepts.decision: Evaluate natural, crime, infrastructure, legal, and operational factors before commitment.
concepts.definition: Choice of location based on threat, access, utilities, neighbors, emergency services, and recovery needs.
concepts.failureExample: A data center is placed in a flood-prone area without alternate capability.
concepts.label: Site Selection

concepts.decision: Separate public, reception, work, restricted, and equipment areas with complementary controls.
concepts.definition: Layered physical zones and safeguards that do not rely on one barrier.
concepts.failureExample: A single badge reader is the only protection for a critical room.
concepts.label: Defense In Depth

concepts.decision: Apply when layout can improve observation and legitimate use without defeating safety or accessibility.
concepts.definition: Use of visibility, lighting, territorial cues, and controlled circulation to reduce opportunity.
concepts.failureExample: A hidden service entrance has poor lighting and no clear boundary.
concepts.label: Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design

concepts.decision: Ensure security barriers, alarms, locks, and shutdown behavior preserve life safety and egress.
concepts.definition: Protection of people and safe operation during normal, emergency, and degraded conditions.
concepts.failureExample: A lockdown prevents occupants from using an emergency exit.
concepts.label: Safety

concepts.decision: Use barriers, lighting, monitoring, signage, and response matched to threat and property.
concepts.definition: Outer boundary controlling approach to a site or protected zone.
concepts.failureExample: A loading dock provides unmonitored direct entry to a restricted area.
concepts.label: Perimeter

concepts.decision: Define purpose, eligible roles, escort rules, access evidence, and emergency behavior.
concepts.definition: Zone requiring authorization and proportional controls because of asset or process consequence.
concepts.failureExample: A contractor uses a shared badge to enter an equipment room.
concepts.label: Restricted Area

concepts.decision: Use when nonemployees need temporary site or restricted-zone access.
concepts.definition: Process for identifying, authorizing, escorting, logging, and removing visitor access.
concepts.failureExample: A visitor badge remains active after a meeting and permits return access.
concepts.label: Visitor Management

concepts.decision: Assess likelihood, consequence, detection, resilience, and recovery by site and asset.
concepts.definition: Risk from utilities, weather, fire, water, temperature, neighbors, or human events.
concepts.failureExample: A server room has no water detection beneath elevated equipment.
concepts.label: Environmental Risk

concepts.decision: Choose by life-safety, security, and operational consequence, then test it.
concepts.definition: Physical control behavior that moves to a safe condition during power or system failure.
concepts.failureExample: A door fails locked during evacuation or fails open into a high-risk area without design review.
concepts.label: Fail Safe

misconceptions.claim: More barriers always mean a more secure facility.
misconceptions.correction: Controls must be proportionate, usable, safe, and integrated with response and continuity requirements.

outcome: Recommend facility design principles for a stated site risk while balancing safety, operations, and protection needs.

sections.body: Assess location, crime and disaster exposure, utilities, access routes, occupancy, critical assets, neighboring tenants, emergency services, and business continuity needs. Use layered zones from public to restricted areas, with proportional barriers and monitoring. Environmental design, visibility, lighting, clear boundaries, and controlled circulation can reduce opportunity while supporting legitimate use and emergency egress.
keyPoints: A facility design must protect people without impeding emergency response.
Layering delays and detects unauthorized movement before critical assets are reached.
sections.title: Design from site risk and function

sections.body: Facility design connects to badges, visitor processes, identity lifecycle, cameras, alarms, guards, network and wiring design, environmental monitoring, incident response, and recovery procedures. A locked room is ineffective if keys, badges, visitors, contractor work, and alarm response are unmanaged. Document responsibilities and test normal, emergency, and degraded operations.
keyPoints: Physical and logical security share identity, monitoring, and response dependencies.
A design is complete only when people can operate it safely and consistently.
sections.title: Integrate physical, technical, and operational controls

sections.body: Facility design begins with asset criticality, people safety, process continuity, threat environment, location, legal or contractual constraints, and business recovery objectives. Layer site perimeter, reception, work areas, restricted zones, equipment rooms, visitor and delivery paths, utilities, environmental resilience, monitoring, response, recovery, and alternate operation. Apply deterrence, delay, detection, assessment, response, recovery, and separation of duties while considering accessibility and operations. Define who approves access and change, how emergencies behave, how evidence is protected, and how the site remains usable after a utility, fire, natural, or human event. Failures include a strong server-room lock with unprotected loading access, a design that traps people during emergency egress, or resilience plans that omit facility-dependent staff and services.
keyPoints: State the protected property, boundary, decision owner, operating evidence, and residual failure mode.
Treat architecture controls as lifecycle commitments: configuration, monitoring, response, maintenance, and recovery determine whether the claim holds.
sections.title: Design a site as layered people, process, environment, and recovery boundaries

notes: The emergency path is available from the inside without requiring normal entry authorization.
Opening the emergency exit raises an alarm; it does not authorize entry from outside.
A blocked or locked egress route is a life-safety failure even when the restricted boundary remains intact.
